accomplished by merely touching, however slightly, the body of the
accused, by the party making the arrest and for that purpose,
although he does not succeed in stopping or holding him even for an
instant; as where the bailiff had tried to arrest one who fought
him off by the fork, the court said, 'If the bailiff had touched
him, that had been an arrest. . . .'"

															A. Cornelius, Search and Seizure 163-164 (2d ed.1930) (footnote
omitted).

															To say that an arrest is effected by the slightest application
of physical force, despite the arrestee's escape, is not to say
that, for Fourth Amendment purposes, there is a continuing arrest during the period of fugitivity. If, for example, Pertoso
had laid his hands upon Hodari to arrest him, but Hodari had broken
away and had then cast away the cocaine, it would hardly be
realistic to say that that disclosure had been made during the
course of an arrest. Cf. 85 U. S. Whitman, 18 Wall. 457, 85 U. S. 471 (1874)
("A seizure is a single act, and not a continuous fact"). The
present case, however, is even one step further removed. It does
not involve the application of any physical force; Hodari was
untouched by Officer Pertoso at the time he discarded the cocaine.
His defense relies instead upon the proposition that a seizure
occurs "when the officer, by means of physical force or show of
authority, has in some way restrained the liberty of a
citizen." Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1 , 392 U. S. 19 , n.
1 (1968) (emphasis added). Hodari contends (and we accept as true
for purposes of this decision) that Pertoso's pursuit qualified as
a "show of authority" Page 499 U. S. 626 calling upon Hodari to halt. The narrow question before us is
whether, with respect to a show of authority as with respect to
application of physical force, a seizure occurs even though the
subject does not yield. We hold that it does not.

															The language of the Fourth Amendment, of course, cannot sustain
respondent's contention. The word "seizure" readily bears the
meaning of a laying on of hands or application of physical force to
restrain movement, even when it is ultimately unsuccessful. ("She
seized the purse-snatcher, but he broke out of her grasp.") It does
not remotely apply, however, to the prospect of a policeman yelling
"Stop, in the name of the law!" at a fleeing form that continues to
flee. That is no seizure. [ Footnote
2 ] Nor can the result respondent wishes to achieve be produced
-- indirectly, as it were -- by suggesting that Pertoso's
uncomplied-with show of authority was a common law arrest, and then
appealing to the principle that all common law arrests are
seizures. An arrest requires either physical force (as
described above) or, where that is absent, submission to the assertion of authority.

															"Mere words will not constitute an arrest, while, on the other
hand, no actual, physical touching is essential. The apparent
inconsistency in the two parts of this statement is explained by
the fact that an assertion of authority and purpose to arrest,
followed by submission of the arrestee, constitutes an arrest.
There can be no arrest Page 499 U. S. 627 without either touching or submission."

															Perkins, The Law of Arrest, 25 Iowa L.Rev. 201, 206 (1940)
(footnotes omitted).

															We do not think it desirable, even as a policy matter, to
stretch the Fourth Amendment beyond its words and beyond the
meaning of arrest, as respondent urges. [ Footnote 3 ] Street pursuits always place the public at
some risk, and compliance with police orders to stop should
therefore be encouraged. Only a few of those orders, we must
presume, will be without adequate basis, and since the addressee
has no ready means of identifying the deficient ones, it almost
invariably is the responsible course to comply. Unlawful orders
will not be deterred, moreover, by sanctioning through the
exclusionary rule those of them that are not obeyed. Since
policemen do not command "Stop!" expecting to be ignored, or give
chase hoping to be outrun, it fully suffices to apply the deterrent
to their genuine, successful seizures.

															Respondent contends that his position is sustained by the
so-called Mendenhall test, formulated by Justice Stewart's
opinion in United States v. Mendenhall, 446 U.
S. 544 , 446 U. S. 554 (1980), and adopted by the Court in later cases, see Michigan
v. Chesternut, 486 U. S. 567 , 486 U. S. 573 (1988); INS v. Delgado, 466 U. S. 210 , 466 U. S. 215 (1984):

															"A person has been 'seized' within the Page 499 U. S. 628 meaning of the Fourth Amendment only if, in view of all the
circumstances surrounding the incident, a reasonable person would
have believed that he was not free to leave."

															446 U.S. at 446 U. S. 554 . See also Florida v. Royer, 460 U.
S. 491 , 460 U. S. 502 (1983) (opinion of WHITE, J.). In seeking to rely upon that test
here, respondent fails to read it carefully. It says that a person
has been seized "only if," not that he has been seized "whenever";
it states a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for seizure -- or, more precisely, for seizure effected
through a "show of authority." Mendenhall establishes that
the test for existence of a "show of authority" is an objective
one: not whether the citizen perceived that he was being ordered to
restrict his movement, but whether the officer's words and actions
would have conveyed that to a reasonable person. Application of
this objective test was the basis for our decision in the other
case principally relied upon by respondent, Chesternut,
supra, where we concluded that the police cruiser's slow
following of the defendant did not convey the message that he was
not free to disregard the police and go about his business. We did
not address in Chesternut, however, the question whether,
if the Mendenhall test was met -- if the message that the
defendant was not free to leave had been conveyed -- a Fourth
Amendment seizure would have occurred. See 486 U.S. at 486 U. S. 577 (KENNEDY, J., concurring).

															Quite relevant to the present case, however, was our decision in Brower v. Inyo County, 489 U. S. 593 , 489 U. S. 596 (1989). In that case, police cars with flashing lights had chased
the decedent for 20 miles -- surely an adequate "show of authority"
-- but he did not stop until his fatal crash into a police-erected
blockade. The issue was whether his death could be held to be the
consequence of an unreasonable seizure in violation of the Fourth
Amendment. We did not even consider the possibility that a seizure
could have occurred during the course of the chase because, as we
explained, that "show of authority" did not produce his stop. Id. at 489 U. S. 597 .
And we discussed Page 499 U. S. 629 ibid., an opinion of Justice Holmes, involving a
situation not much different from the present case, where revenue
agents had picked up containers dropped by moonshiners whom they
were pursuing without adequate warrant. The containers were not
excluded as the product of an unlawful seizure because

															"[t]he defendant's own acts, and those of his associates,
disclosed the jug, the jar and the bottle -- and there was no
seizure in the sense of the law when the officers examined the
contents of each after they had been abandoned." Nester v. United States, 265 U. S.
57 , 265 U. S. 58 (1924). The same is true here.

															In sum, assuming that Pertoso's pursuit in the present case
constituted a "show of authority" enjoining Hodari to halt, since
Hodari did not comply with that injunction, he was not seized until
he was tackled. The cocaine abandoned while he was running was, in
this case, not the fruit of a seizure, and his motion to exclude
evidence of it was properly denied. We reverse the decision of the
California Court of Appeal, and remand for further proceedings not
inconsistent with this opinion. It is so ordered [ Footnote 1 ]

															California conceded below that Officer Pertoso did not have the
"reasonable suspicion" required to justify stopping Hodari, see
Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1 (1968).
That it would be unreasonable to stop, for brief inquiry, young men
who scatter in panic upon the mere sighting of the police is not
self-evident, and arguably contradicts proverbial common sense. See Proverbs 28:1 ("The wicked flee when no man
pursueth"). We do not decide that point here, but rely entirely
upon the State's concession.

															[ Footnote 2 ]

															For this simple reason -- which involves neither
"logic-chopping," post at 499 U. S. 646 ,
nor any arcane knowledge of legal history -- it is irrelevant that
English law proscribed "an unlawful attempt to take a
presumptively innocent person into custody." Post at 499 U. S. 631 .
We have consulted the common law to explain the meaning of seizure
-- and, contrary to the dissent's portrayal, to expand, rather than
contract, that meaning (since one would not normally think that the
mere touching of a person would suffice). But neither usage nor
common law tradition makes an attempted seizure a seizure.
The common law may have made an attempted seizure unlawful in
certain circumstances; but it made many things unlawful, very few
of which were elevated to constitutional proscriptions.

															[ Footnote 3 ]

															Nor have we ever done so. The dissent is wrong in saying that Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1 (1968)
"broadened the range of encounters . . . encompassed within the
term seizure,'" post at 499 U. S. 635 . Terry unquestionably involved conduct that would
constitute a common law seizure; its novelty (if any) was in
expanding the acceptable justification for such a seizure
beyond probable cause. The dissent is correct that Katz v.
United States, 389 U. S. 347 (1967) "unequivocally reject[s] the notion that the common law of
arrest defines the limits of the term `seizure' in the Fourth
Amendment," post at 499 U. S. 637 .
But we do not assert that it defines the limits of the term
"seizure"; only that it defines the limits of a seizure of the
person. What Katz stands for is the proposition that
items which could not be subject to seizure at common law
( e.g., telephone conversations) can be seized under the
Fourth Amendment. That is quite different from saying that what
constitutes an arrest (a seizure of the person) has
changed. JUSTICE STEVENS, with whom JUSTICE MARSHALL joins,
dissenting.

															The Court's narrow construction of the word "seizure" represents
a significant, and in my view, unfortunate, departure from prior
case law construing the Fourth Amendment. [ Footnote 2/1 ] Almost a quarter of a century ago, in two
landmark cases -- one broadening the protection of individual
privacy, [ Footnote 2/2 ] and the
other broadening the powers of law enforcement officers [ Footnote 2/3 ] -- we rejected the method of
Fourth Amendment analysis that Page 499 U. S. 630 today's majority endorses. In particular, the Court now adopts a
definition of "seizure" that is unfaithful to a long line of Fourth
Amendment cases. Even if the Court were defining seizure for the
first time, which it is not, the definition that it chooses today
is profoundly unwise. In its decision, the Court assumes, without
acknowledging, that a police officer may now fire his weapon at an
innocent citizen and not implicate the Fourth Amendment -- as long
as he misses his target.

															For the purposes of decision, the following propositions are not
in dispute. First, when Officer Pertoso began his pursuit of
respondent, [ Footnote 2/4 ] the
officer did not have a lawful basis for either stopping or
arresting respondent. See App. 138-140; ante at 499 U. S. 623 ,
n. 1. Second, the officer's chase amounted to a "show of force" as
soon as respondent saw the officer nearly upon him. See
ante at 499 U. S.
625 -626, 499 U. S. 629 .
Third, the act of discarding the rock of cocaine was the direct
consequence of the show of force. See Pet. for Cert.
48-49, 52. Fourth, as the Court correctly demonstrates, no common
law arrest occurred until the officer tackled respondent. See
ante at 499 U. S.
624 -625. Thus, the Court is quite right in concluding
that the abandonment of the rock was not the fruit of a common law
arrest.

															It is equally clear, however, that, if the officer had succeeded
in touching respondent before he dropped the rock -- Page 499 U. S. 631 even if he did not subdue him -- an arrest would have occurred.
[ Footnote 2/5 ] See ante at 499 U. S.
624 -625, 499 U. S. 626 .
In that event (assuming the touching precipitated the abandonment),
the evidence would have been the fruit of an unlawful common law
arrest. The distinction between the actual case and the
hypothetical case is the same as the distinction between the common
law torts of assault and battery -- a touching converts the former
into the latter. [ Footnote 2/6 ]
Although the distinction between assault and battery was important
for pleading purposes, see 2 J. Chitty, Pleading
*372-*376, the distinction should not take on constitutional
dimensions. The Court mistakenly allows this common law distinction
to define its interpretation of the Fourth Amendment.

															At the same time, the Court fails to recognize the existence of
another, more telling, common law distinction -- the distinction
between an arrest and an attempted arrest. As the Court teaches us,
the distinction between battery and assault was critical to a
correct understanding of the common law of arrest. See
ante at 499 U. S. 626 ("An arrest requires either physical force . . . or, where
that is absent, submission to the assertion of
authority"). However, the facts of this case do not describe an
actual arrest, but rather, an unlawful attempt to take a
presumptively innocent person into custody. Such an Page 499 U. S. 632 attempt was unlawful at common law. [ Footnote 2/7 ] Thus, if the Court wants to define the
scope of the Fourth Amendment based on the common law, it should
look, not to the common law of arrest, but to the common law of
attempted arrest, according to the facts of this case.

															The first question, then, is whether the common law should
define the scope of the outer boundaries of the constitutional
protection against unreasonable seizures. Even if, contrary to
settled precedent, traditional common law analysis were
controlling, it would still be necessary to decide whether the
unlawful attempt to make an arrest should be considered a seizure
within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment, and whether the
exclusionary rule should apply to unlawful attempts. I The Court today takes a narrow view of "seizure," which is at
odds with the broader view adopted by this Court almost 25 years
ago. In Katz v. United States, 389 U.
S. 347 (1967), the Court considered whether electronic
surveillance conducted "without any trespass and without the
seizure of any material object fell outside the ambit of the
Constitution." Id. at 389 U. S. 353 .
Over Justice Black's powerful dissent, we rejected that "narrow
view" of the Fourth Amendment, and held that electronic
eavesdropping is a "search and seizure" within the meaning of the
Amendment. Id. at 389 U. S. 353 -354. We thus endorsed the position
expounded by two of the dissenting Justices in Olmstead v.
United States, 277 U. S. 438 (1928): Page 499 U. S. 633 "Time and again, this Court, in giving effect to the principle
underlying the Fourth Amendment, has refused to place an unduly
literal construction upon it." Id. at 277 U. S. 476 (Brandeis, J., dissenting).

															"The direct operation or literal meaning of the words used do
not measure the purpose or scope of its provisions. Under the
principles established and applied by this Court, the Fourth
Amendment safeguards against all evils that are like and equivalent
to those embraced within the ordinary meaning of its words." Id. at 277 U. S. 488 (Butler, J., dissenting).

															Writing for the Court in Katz, JUSTICE Stewart explained:

															"Thus, although a closely divided Court supposed in Olmstead that surveillance without any trespass and
without the seizure of any material object fell outside the ambit
of the Constitution, we have since departed from the narrow view on
which that decision rested. Indeed, we have expressly held that the
Fourth Amendment governs not only the seizure of tangible items,
but extends as well to the recording of oral statements, overheard
without any 'technical trespass under . . . local property law.' Silverman v. United States, 365 U. S.
505 , 365 U. S. 511 . Once this
much is acknowledged, and once it is recognized that the Fourth
Amendment protects people -- and not simply 'areas' -- against
unreasonable searches and seizures, it becomes clear that the reach
of that Amendment cannot turn upon the presence or absence of a
physical intrusion into any given enclosure."

															"We conclude that the underpinnings of Olmstead and Goldman
\[v. U.S. , 316 U. S. 129 (1942),] have been
so eroded by our subsequent decisions that the 'trespass' doctrine
there enunciated can no longer be regarded as controlling. The
Government's activities in electronically listening to and
recording the petitioner's words violated the privacy upon which he
justifiably relied while using the telephone Page 499 U. S. 634 booth, and thus constituted a 'search and seizure' within the
meaning of the Fourth Amendment. The fact that the electronic
device employed to achieve that end did not happen to penetrate the
wall of the booth can have no constitutional significance."

															"The question remaining for decision, then, is whether the
search and seizure conducted in this case complied with
constitutional standards."

															389 U.S. at 389 U. S.
353 -354. Significantly, in the Katz opinion,
the Court repeatedly used the word "seizure" to describe the
process of recording sounds that could not possibly have been the
subject of a common law seizure. See id. at 389 U. S. 356 , 389 U. S.
357 .

															Justice Black's reasoning, which was rejected by the Court in
1967, is remarkably similar to the reasoning adopted by the Court
today. After criticizing "language-stretching judges," 389 U.S. at 389 U. S. 366 ,
Justice Black wrote:

															"I do not deny that common sense requires and that this Court
often has said that the Bill of Rights' safeguards should be given
a liberal construction. This principle, however, does not justify
construing the search and seizure amendment as applying to
eavesdropping or the 'seizure' of conversations." Id. at 389 U. S.
366 -367.

															"Since I see no way in which the words of the Fourth Amendment
can be construed to apply to eavesdropping, that closes the matter
for me. In interpreting the Bill of Rights, I willingly go as far
as a liberal construction of the language takes me, but I simply
cannot in good conscience give a meaning to words which they have
never before been thought to have and which they certainly do not
have in common ordinary usage. I will not distort the words of the
Amendment in order to 'keep the Constitution up to date' or 'to
bring it into harmony with the times.' It was never meant that this
Court have such power, which in effect would make us a continuously
functioning constitutional convention." Id. at 389 U. S.
373 . Page 499 U. S. 635 The expansive construction of the word "seizure" in the Katz case provided an appropriate predicate for the
Court's holding in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S.
1 (1968), the following year. [ Footnote 2/8 ] Prior to Terry, the Fourth
Amendment proscribed any seizure of the person that was not
supported by the same probable cause showing that would justify a
custodial arrest. [ Footnote 2/9 ] See Dunaway v. New York, 442 U. S. 200 , 442 U. S.
207 -209 (1979). Given the fact that street encounters
between citizens and police officers "are incredibly rich in
diversity," Terry, 392 U.S. at 392 U. S. 13 , the
Court recognized the need for flexibility, and held that
"reasonable" suspicion -- a quantum of proof less demanding than
probable cause -- was adequate to justify a stop for investigatory
purposes. Id. at 392 U. S. 21 -22.
As a corollary to the lesser justification for the stop, the Court
necessarily concluded that the word "seizure" in the Fourth
Amendment encompasses official restraints on individual freedom
that fall short of a common law arrest. Thus, Terry broadened the range of encounters between the police and the
citizen encompassed within the term "seizure," while at the same
time, lowering the standard of proof necessary to justify a "stop"
in the newly expanded category of seizures Page 499 U. S. 636 now covered by the Fourth Amendment. [ Footnote 2/10 ] The Court explained:

															"Our first task is to establish at what point in this encounter
the Fourth Amendment becomes relevant. That is, we must decide
whether and when Officer McFadden 'seized' Terry and whether and
when he conducted a 'search.' There is some suggestion in the use
of such terms as 'stop' and 'frisk' that such police conduct is
outside the purview of the Fourth Amendment because neither action
rises to the level of a 'search' or 'seizure' within the meaning of
the Constitution. We emphatically reject this notion. It is quite
plain that the Fourth Amendment governs 'seizures' of the person
which do not eventuate in a trip to the station house and
prosecution for crime -- 'arrests' in traditional terminology. It
must be recognized that, whenever a police officer accosts an
individual and restrains his freedom to walk away, he has 'seized'
that person." Id. at 392 U. S. 16 (footnote omitted).

															"The distinctions of classical 'stop-and-frisk' theory thus
serve to divert attention from the central inquiry under the Fourth
Amendment -- the reasonableness in all the circumstances of the
particular governmental invasion of a citizen's personal security.
'Search' and 'seizure' are not talismans. We therefore reject the
notions that the Fourth Amendment does not come into play at all as
a limitation upon police conduct if the officers stop short of
something called a 'technical arrest' or a 'full-blown
search.'" Id. at 392 U. S. 19 . Page 499 U. S. 637 The decisions in Katz and Terry unequivocally
reject the notion that the common law of arrest defines the limits
of the term "seizure" in the Fourth Amendment. In Katz, the Court abandoned the narrow view that would have limited a
seizure to a material object, and instead, held that the Fourth
Amendment extended to the recording of oral statements. And in Terry, the Court abandoned its traditional view that a
seizure under the Fourth Amendment required probable cause, and
instead, expanded the definition of a seizure to include an
investigative stop made on less than probable cause. Thus, the
major premise underpinning the majority's entire analysis today --
that the common law of arrest should define the term "seizure" for
Fourth Amendment purposes, see ante at 499 U. S.
624 -625 -- is seriously flawed. The Court mistakenly
hearkens back to common law, while ignoring the expansive approach
that the Court has taken in Fourth Amendment analysis since Katz and Terry. [ Footnote 2/11 ] II The Court fares no better when it tries to explain why the
proper definition of the term "seizure" has been an open question
until today. In Terry, in addition to stating that a
seizure occurs "whenever a police officer accosts an individual and
restrains his freedom to walk away," 392 U.S. at 392 U. S. 16 , the
Court noted that a seizure occurs "when the officer, by means of
physical force or show of authority, has in some way restrained the
liberty of a citizen. . . ." Id. at 392 U. S. 19 , n.
16. The touchstone of a seizure is the restraint of an individual's
personal liberty " in some way. " Ibid. (emphasis
added). [ Footnote 2/12 ] Today the
Court's reaction to respondent's reliance on Terry Page 499 U. S. 638 is to demonstrate that, in "show of force" cases, no common law
arrest occurs unless the arrestee submits. See
ante at 499 U. S.
626 -627. That answer, however, is plainly insufficient,
given the holding in Terry that the Fourth Amendment
applies to stops that need not be justified by probable cause in
the absence of a full-blown arrest.

															In United States v. Mendenhall, 446 U.
S. 544 (1980), the Court

															"adhere[d] to the view that a person is 'seized' only when, by
means of physical force or a show of authority, his freedom of
movement is restrained." Id. at 446 U. S. 553 .
The Court looked to whether the citizen who is questioned "remains
free to disregard the questions and walk away," and, if she is able
to do so, then "there has been no intrusion upon that person's
liberty or privacy" that would require some "particularized and
objective justification" under the Constitution. Id. at 446 U. S. 554 .
The test for a "seizure," as formulated by the Court in Mendenhall, was whether, "in view of all of the
circumstances surrounding the incident, a reasonable person would
have believed that he was not free to leave." Ibid. Examples of seizures include

															"the threatening presence of several officers, the display of a
weapon by an officer, some physical touching of the person of the
citizen, or the use of language or tone of voice indicating that
compliance with the officer's request might be compelled." Ibid. The Court's unwillingness today to adhere to the
"reasonable person" standard, as formulated by Justice Stewart in Mendenhall, marks an unnecessary departure from Fourth
Amendment case law.

															The Court today draws the novel conclusion that even though no
seizure can occur unless the Mendenhall reasonable person standard is met, see ante at 499 U. S. 628 ,
the fact that the standard has been met does not necessarily mean
that a seizure has occurred. See ibid. ( Mendenhall "states a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for seizure . . . effected Page 499 U. S. 639 through a show of authority' "). If it were true that a
seizure requires more than whether a reasonable person felt free to
leave, then the following passage from the Court's opinion in INS v. Delgado, 466 U. S. 210 (1984), is at best, seriously misleading: "As we have noted elsewhere:"

															"Obviously, not all personal intercourse between policemen and
citizens involves 'seizures' of persons. Only when the officer, by
means of physical force or show of authority, has restrained the
liberty of a citizen may we conclude that a 'seizure' has
occurred."

															" Terry v. Ohio, supra, at 392 U. S.
19 , n. 16. While applying such a test is relatively
straightforward in a situation resembling a traditional arrest, see Dunaway v. New York, 442 U. S. 200 , 442 U. S.
212 -216 (1979), the protection against unreasonable
seizures also extends to 'seizures that involve only a brief
detention short of traditional arrest.' United States v.
Brignoni-Ponce, 422 U. S. 873 , 422 U. S.
878 (1975). What has evolved from our cases is a
determination that an initially consensual encounter between a
police officer and a citizen can be transformed into a seizure or
detention within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment, 'if, in view
of all the circumstances surrounding the incident, a reasonable
person would have believed that he was not free to leave.' Mendenhall, supra, [446 U.S.] at 446 U. S.
554 (footnote omitted); see Florida v. Royer, 460 U. S.
491 , 460 U. S. 502 (1983)
(plurality opinion)." Id. 466 U.S. at 466 U. S.
215 .

															More importantly, in Florida v. Royer, 460 U.
S. 491 (1983), a plurality of the Court adopted Justice

															"may not be detained even momentarily without
reasonable, objective grounds for doing so; and his refusal to
listen or answer does not, without more, furnish those grounds. United States v. Mendenhall, supra, at 446 U. S.
556 (opinion of Stewart, J.)."

															460 U.S. at 460 U. S. 498 (emphasis added). The rule looks, not to the subjective perceptions
of the person questioned, but rather, to the objective
characteristics of the encounter that may suggest whether a
reasonable person would have felt free to leave.

															Even though momentary, a seizure occurs whenever an objective
evaluation of a police officer's show of force conveys the message

That the Court understood the Mendenhall definition as

															"A 'seizure' of property occurs when there is some meaningful

															Finally, it is noteworthy that, in Michigan v.

In our opinion, we described Justice Stewart's analysis in Mendenhall as "a test to be applied in determining whether a person has been "seized" within the meaning of the Fourth
Amendment,'" and noted that "[t]he Court has since embraced this
test." Ibid. Moreover, in commenting on the virtues of the
test, we explained that it focused on the police officer's
conduct: "The test's objective standard -- looking to the reasonable
man's interpretation of the conduct in question -- allows the
police to determine in advance whether the conduct contemplated

argument in Chesternut, Professor LaFave observed:

															"The 'free to leave' concept, in other words, has nothing to do
with a particular suspect's choice to flee rather than submit or
with his assessment of the probability of successful flight. Were

from constitutional scrutiny the initial stages of the contact

2/14 ] Whereas, in Mendenhall, there was

implicated at the earlier or the later moment.

appropriate to note that the same issue would arise if the show of
force took the form of a command to "freeze," a warning shot, or
the sound of sirens accompanied by a patrol car's flashing lights.

626 -627. One consequence of this conclusion is that the

not depend on the character of the victim's evasive action. The

tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Strategic Intent:**
As a senior appellate litigator relying on enterprise AI UIs, you face a critical operational hazard: AI-generated summaries routinely ignore concurring and dissenting opinions. In high-stakes litigation, a past dissent often forms the blueprint for a future winning argument or a Supreme Court reversal. Your objective is to bypass the synthetic summary entirely and parse the raw, monolithic court document to extract non-majority opinions, decipher their fundamental legal divergence from the majority, and transform them into proactive adversarial strategies.

**Data Weighting:**
- **Primary Ground Truth:** The `document` column. This is your sole source of factual and legal truth.
- **Ignored Noise:** The `summary` column. Treat it as non-existent for this task to avoid contamination by prior AI hallucinations or omissions.
- **Categorical Context:** Use the `category` and `case` columns to frame the legal domain.

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Document Scanning & Justice Identification:** Parse the full `document` text specifically hunting for headers or language indicating a concurrence or dissent (e.g., "Justice X, dissenting", "Justice Y, concurring in part").
2. **Divergence Mapping:** Isolate the exact legal, procedural, or constitutional rationale where the dissenting/concurring Justice breaks from the majority opinion. Identify the specific tests, precedents, or constitutional clauses invoked.
3. **Factual Extraction:** Pull 1-2 direct, unedited verbatim quotes from the dissent/concurrence that encapsulate the core of the disagreement.
4. **Strategic Application Synthesis:** Project how this dissenting logic could be weaponized by opposing counsel in a future case within the same `category`, or how it could be used to narrow the scope of the majority's holding.

**Tone & Style:**
- Objective, razor-sharp legal prose.
- Utilize precise terminology (e.g., *dicta*, *stare decisis*, *curtilage*, *strict scrutiny*).
- Output must read like a senior partner's strategy memo.

**Content Requirements:**
- Formal Case Title and Legal Category.
- Explicit identification of the dissenting/concurring Justices.
- The "Core Divergence" (a 2-3 sentence distillation of the legal disagreement).
- Verbatim quotes properly attributed.
- "Litigation Strategy Vector": A paragraph detailing how to leverage this opinion in court.

**Constraint Checklist & Negative Constraints:**
- DO NOT refer to or rely upon the AI-generated `summary`.
- DO NOT hallucinate legal principles or blend the majority holding with the dissent.
- DO NOT use conversational filler (e.g., "Here is the analysis," "It is important to note").
- DO NOT summarize the facts of the case unless strictly necessary to explain the dissent.

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Extraction Accuracy:** Zero hallucinations; all extracted logic strictly matches the provided raw document.
2. **Strategic Utility:** The synthesized litigation strategy is plausible, legally sound, and directly actionable for an appellate lawyer.

tasks_info.task_name: Adversarial Summary Audit & Unassailable Precedent Briefing
tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Strategic Intent:**
You are a Principal Legal Strategist conducting a high-fidelity audit of synthetic AI outputs. Your persona relies on AI chatbots but is hyper-aware that the provided `summary` may oversimplify complex rulings, omit crucial multi-part legal tests, or hallucinate absolute rules where exceptions exist. A single hallucination in court is fatal. Your objective is to pit the synthetic `summary` against the ground-truth `document` in an adversarial audit, expose its fatal flaws, and synthesize an "Unassailable Precedent Brief" that a litigator can unequivocally trust at trial.

**Data Weighting:**
- **Target for Audit (Noise/Vulnerability):** The `summary` column. Treat this as a hostile, potentially flawed document produced by a junior associate prone to errors.
- **Absolute Ground Truth:** The `document` column. Every claim must be tethered to this text.

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Deconstruct the Summary:** Break down the provided `summary` into atomic legal claims (e.g., "The court ruled X," "The facts were Y").
2. **Adversarial Cross-Reference:** Scan the raw `document` to verify, debunk, or nuance each atomic claim. Actively hunt for omitted legal thresholds, multi-prong tests, or caveats that the summary failed to mention.
3. **Discrepancy Reporting:** Draft a "Summary Audit Log" detailing exactly what the synthetic summary hallucinated, oversimplified, or dangerously omitted.
4. **Holding Extraction:** Formulate the *true* holding of the court. If a specific legal standard or test was established (e.g., the O'Brien test, the Katz standard), extract its exact parameters.
5. **Vulnerability Analysis:** Based on the true holding, write a "Precedent Vulnerability" assessment. Identify the factual boundaries of the ruling to show opposing counsel's most likely path to distinguish their future cases from this precedent.

**Tone & Style:**
- Highly critical, analytical, and authoritative.
- Structurally dense but easily scannable (use markdown tables or bulleted legal prongs).
- Zero tolerance for ambiguity.

**Content Requirements:**
1. **Summary Audit Log:** Specific critiques of the `summary` column's inadequacies.
2. **The Unassailable Holding:** The precise legal rule established, including all caveats and exceptions.
3. **Governing Legal Framework/Test:** Exact articulation of the legal test applied by the majority.
4. **Precedent Vulnerability Analysis:** How the precedent can be attacked or distinguished based strictly on the text.

**Constraint Checklist & Negative Constraints:**
- DO NOT accept any premise in the `summary` without explicitly validating it against the `document`.
- DO NOT paraphrase multi-part legal tests; they must reflect the rigid structure found in the text.
- DO NOT output standard boilerplate introductions or conclusions.
- DO NOT invent secondary effects outside the four corners of the provided text.

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Audit Rigor:** Did the AI successfully identify critical nuances or omissions in the synthetic summary?
2. **Exactitude of Precedent:** Is the governing legal test perfectly accurate and immune to hallucination?
3. **Adversarial Value:** Does the vulnerability analysis provide a highly specific, text-grounded roadmap for distinguishing the case?

tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Strategic Intent:** 
Your primary objective is to transform complex, variable-length legal data into highly predictable, low-latency UI components. The user interface requires snappy, instant-loading case cards, but the extreme variance in the dataset's document lengths (up to 700,000 characters) causes unacceptable API timeouts, unpredictable token costs, and severe latency spikes. To circumvent this, you will act as a 'Semantic Truncator,' bypassing the massive raw documents and relying exclusively on the synthetic `summary` and `category` fields to generate ultra-concise, consumer-friendly metadata payloads. This allows the non-lawyer product team to maintain strict control over output tokens while delivering immediate value to the end-user.

**Data Weighting:**
- **Ground Truth:** Treat the `summary` column as the absolute factual baseline for this specific task.
- **Categorical Lens:** Use the `category` column to frame the context of the output.
- **Noise/Omission:** Completely ignore the `document` field to guarantee flat token usage and zero latency spikes.
- **Null Handling:** If `summary` is empty or incoherent, output a standardized fallback error string: 'Summary unavailable for dynamic processing.'

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Ingestion & Constraint Mapping:** Read the `summary` and `category`. Calculate an internal baseline for the maximum output length (strict limit of 100 tokens).
2. **Entity & Conflict Extraction:** Identify the core opposing parties (A vs. B) and the central legal friction point.
3. **Resolution Identification:** Determine the final ruling or outcome based solely on the synthetic summary.
4. **UX Translation:** Strip away all archaic legal jargon (e.g., 'certiorari', 'ex parte', 'in personam'). Translate the conflict and resolution into an 8th-grade reading level, prioritizing cognitive ease for a layperson.
5. **JSON Structuring:** Format the synthesized data into a predefined, highly rigid JSON schema designed for immediate frontend rendering.

**Tone & Style:**
- Ultra-concise, accessible, and objective.
- UX-friendly and conversational yet authoritative.
- Vocabulary must be restricted to plain English; no Latin maxims unless immediately defined in four words or less.

**Content Requirements:**
- `tl_dr`: A maximum 15-word summary of the case.
- `who_won`: A 2-to-4 word string identifying the victor.
- `ux_impact_statement`: A one-sentence explanation of why this ruling matters to the average citizen.
- `estimated_reading_time`: A calculated integer representing seconds to read the output.

**Constraint Checklist:**
- DO NOT exceed 100 output tokens under any circumstances.
- DO NOT reference the raw `document` field.
- DO NOT hallucinate facts, dates, or rulings not explicitly present in the `summary`.
- DO NOT use verbose transition phrases (e.g., 'In this case', 'The summary states').

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Token Efficiency:** Output strictly adheres to the <100 token constraint, minimizing API cost.
2. **Accessibility:** The Flesch-Kincaid readability score aligns with a general consumer audience (8th-grade level).
3. **Schema Adherence:** The JSON output maps perfectly to the requested keys without malformed syntax.

tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: By intentionally isolating the `summary` and ignoring the massive `document` column, we bypass the context window variance completely. tasks_info.task_name: Adversarial Summary Verification and Progressive Disclosure Mapping
tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Strategic Intent:** 
As an expert system bridging UX engineering and legal verification, your mission is to act as an adversarial safeguard. The dataset contains synthetic summaries generated by an earlier model, which poses a severe risk of inherited AI hallucinations, bias, and critical omissions. Furthermore, the non-lawyer persona designing this system cannot manually verify 'deep legal truths.' You must forensically audit the synthetic `summary` against a targeted sampling of the raw `document`. Once audited, you will engineer a 'Progressive Disclosure' payload. This technique optimizes user retention and latency by providing an instantly loadable, verified micro-abstract (Tier 1), while reserving the heavier, nuanced legal context (Tier 2) for a delayed, user-initiated API call.

**Data Weighting:**
- **Ground Truth:** The `document` is the absolute, unimpeachable source of truth.
- **Suspect Baseline:** The `summary` is highly suspect. Treat it as a hostile input requiring verification.
- **Noise Filtering:** Discard procedural boilerplate, footnote citations, and jurisdictional throat-clearing within the `document` to preserve your attention mechanism for the core 'holding' (the final court decision).

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Targeted Scanning:** Scan the massive `document` specifically for the 'Holding', 'Conclusion', or 'Held:' sections. Ignore historical preamble.
2. **Adversarial Audit:** Cross-reference your findings with the provided `summary`. Actively search for contradictions, hallucinated precedents, or nuanced legal triggers that the synthetic summary oversimplified or omitted.
3. **Forensic Flagging:** If a discrepancy is found, generate a `hallucination_warning` detailing the exact delta between the raw text and the synthetic summary.
4. **Progressive Disclosure Synthesis (Tier 1):** Generate an ultra-lightweight (max 30 tokens) verified abstract. This is the zero-latency payload the UI will load by default.
5. **Progressive Context Synthesis (Tier 2):** Generate a structured, 150-token analysis of the legal precedent and its real-world business/societal implications. This is the lazy-loaded payload.
6. **Cost-Benefit Scoring:** Output a float value from 0.0 to 1.0 representing the 'Legal Density Score' to help the UX designer understand how cognitively heavy the Tier 2 text is.

**Tone & Style:**
- Forensic, highly analytical, and structurally rigid.
- Expert-to-expert communication: write as a Principal Engineer advising a UX Lead.
- Confident, definitive, and zero-fluff.

**Content Requirements:**
- `hallucination_flag`: Boolean (true/false).
- `audit_report`: 1-sentence explanation of any detected bias or hallucination.
- `tier_1_micro_abstract`: <30 tokens, verified core truth.
- `tier_2_deep_context`: <150 tokens, categorized implications.
- `legal_density_score`: Float between 0.0 and 1.0.

**Constraint Checklist:**
- DO NOT attempt to summarize the entire 700,000-character document; locate the 'Holding' to avoid token exhaustion.
- DO NOT provide legal advice or use prescriptive language (e.g., 'users should do X').
- DO NOT output unverified claims; if the document is too dense to verify the summary, set `hallucination_flag` to true and note the ambiguity.

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Adversarial Precision:** Successfully identifies discrepancies between the raw document and the synthetic summary without false positives.
2. **Architectural Adherence:** Strict compliance with the Progressive Disclosure token limits (Tier 1 < 30 tokens; Tier 2 < 150 tokens) to ensure latency optimization.
3. **Persona Alignment:** The output explicitly bridges the gap between deep legal complexity and front-end UX design, providing actionable metrics like the density score.

tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This tackles both the persona's lack of legal expertise and their strict UX constraints. By forcing the LLM to forensically compare the `document` holding to the synthetic `summary`, we catch inherited AI biases without needing a human lawyer. It then repackages the verified truth into a 'Progressive Disclosure' structure. ### Strategic Intent
Your mission is to perform high-fidelity triage on Supreme Court rulings for a time-constrained Corporate Risk Officer. Because the provided synthetic summaries often lack industry-specific nuance or may contain hallucinations, you must validate the summary against the raw court document. You will then translate the abstract legal `category` into a concrete corporate risk parameter, providing a rapid, auditable brief that allows the user to decide if immediate policy changes are necessary.

### Data Weighting
*   **`document`**: The ultimate ground truth. Use this to fact-check and anchor your analysis.
*   **`summary`**: Treat as a highly suspect baseline. Your job is to audit it.
*   **`category`**: Use as a directional compass, but translate it into corporate terminology.
*   **`case`**: Use strictly for formal identification.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1.  **Summary Audit:** Cross-reference the synthetic `summary` against the raw `document`. Identify any material hallucinations, missing context, or overly broad legal generalizations.
2.  **Categorical Translation:** Analyze the legal `category` (e.g., 'Search & Seizure' or 'Taxes') and map it to a specific Corporate Department or Risk Vector (e.g., 'Workplace Privacy/IT Monitoring' or 'Travel Expense Compliance').
3.  **Risk Extraction:** Isolate the practical business ruling from the `document`. What can a company legally do, or what are they expressly forbidden from doing, based on this verdict?
4.  **Triage Output Generation:** Synthesize your findings into a bottom-line-up-front (BLUF) briefing.

### Tone & Style
*   Executive, pragmatic, and heavily structured.
*   Avoid arcane legal theory, Latin phrases (unless legally unavoidable like *certiorari*, which should be briefly defined), or procedural trial history. 
*   Speak directly to a corporate policy-maker.

### Content Requirements
*   **Case Identifier:** Formal name of the case.
*   **Summary Audit Status:** A pass/fail grade of the provided synthetic summary with a 1-sentence justification.
*   **Corporate Risk Mapping:** The translated risk category.
*   **Operational Impact:** 2-3 bullet points detailing the immediate corporate realities (e.g., 'Employee expense policies must explicitly mandate overnight stays to qualify for deduction.').

### Constraint Checklist
*   DO NOT output raw JSON or code snippets; the persona has zero API knowledge.
*   DO NOT summarize dissenting opinions unless they specifically highlight a loophole relevant to corporate risk.
*   DO NOT advise the user to 'consult a lawyer'—they already know this. Provide the operational baseline.

### Evaluation Rubric
1.  **Audit Accuracy:** Effectively identifies gaps or verifies the synthetic summary using the ground-truth document.
2.  **Corporate Relevance:** Successfully strips away trial mechanics and translates the legal category into a highly relevant corporate risk vector.
3.  **Brevity:** Output is skimmable, structured, and respects the time constraints of the persona.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your mission is to formulate a preemptive, board-ready compliance strategy based on complex Supreme Court mandates. You will bypass the synthetic summary entirely, diving deep into the raw court opinion to identify the structural boundaries of the law. You must then employ adversarial reasoning to stress-test standard corporate operating procedures against this new legal boundary, simulating edge-case vulnerabilities and delivering a strategic audit playbook.

### Data Weighting
*   **`document`**: The sole source of truth. You must extract the precise mechanics of the ruling from this text.
*   **`category` & `case`**: Use for framing and titling the strategy document.
*   **`summary`**: IGNORE COMPLETELY. Do not allow synthetic biases or shallow abstractions to influence your risk modeling.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1.  **Core Mandate Isolation:** Scan the `document` for the strict legal boundary established by the majority opinion. Isolate the precise operational test the Court applies (e.g., the 'sleep or rest' rule for deductions, or the 'general public use' standard for thermal surveillance).
2.  **Friction Mapping (Adversarial Reasoning):** Cross-reference this legal boundary with standard corporate practices. Where do normal business operations (e.g., HR monitoring, IT security sweeps, aggressive tax write-offs) intersect with this ruling? Identify the 'grey areas'.
3.  **Secondary Effects Simulation:** Predict the downstream business consequences of this ruling. If a company enforces this mandate, what happens to IT budgets, employee friction, or marketing capabilities?
4.  **Audit Playbook Formulation:** Draft a highly specific, 3-point strategy to audit existing corporate policies and mitigate the newly identified risks.

### Tone & Style
*   Authoritative, risk-averse, and highly strategic.
*   Focus on 'First Principles' thinking and systemic risk mitigation.

tasks_info.task_name: The Layman's Docket: Core Conflict & Bottom Line Translator
tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your mission is to act as a crucial editorial bridge between archaic, impenetrable legal text and a fast-paced news audience. The user is a skilled journalistic editor who operates under tight deadlines and is easily overwhelmed by raw, unstructured legal data. Your goal is to transform highly technical, verbose Supreme Court cases (often spanning tens of thousands of words) into accessible, engaging, and highly accurate news briefs. You must simplify without sacrificing the precise legal meaning of the ruling.

### Data Weighting
* **`summary`**: Use this as your high-level map to quickly understand the case context. However, treat it as secondary "synthetic" noise.
* **`document`**: This is your absolute GROUND TRUTH. You must extract the exact constitutional or statutory anchor from this text.
* **`category` & `case`**: Use these strictly for thematic tagging and titling.
* **`case_link`**: Ignore completely.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Isolate the Core Paradox**: Scan the `document` (prioritizing the syllabus or introductory paragraphs) to identify the fundamental human or legal conflict (Who vs. Who, and what fundamental right is at stake?).
2. **De-Jargonize the Law**: Identify the specific law or constitutional amendment in question. Translate any Latin terms (e.g., *certiorari*, *habeas corpus*) or archaic phrasings into modern 8th-grade-level equivalents.
3. **Extract the Ruling**: What did the Court actually decide? Distill the majority opinion's primary rationale.
4. **Draft the 'Bottom Line'**: Synthesize the above into a 2-3 sentence journalistic takeaway that answers the reader's ultimate question: "Why does this matter to the average citizen?"

### Tone & Style
* **Voice**: Journalistic, authoritative, yet highly accessible.
* **Vocabulary**: AP Style. Punchy and narrative-driven. No academic bloat.

### Content Requirements
* **Headline**: A catchy, 6-8 word news headline.
* **The Conflict**: A 2-sentence summary of the original dispute.
* **The Ruling**: A 1-sentence translation of the Supreme Court's decision.
* **The Bottom Line**: A 2-sentence impact statement.
* **Analogy**: One simple, everyday analogy explaining the legal principle.

### Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
1. DO NOT hallucinate secondary impacts not explicitly supported by the `document`.
2. DO NOT use archaic legal terminology without immediate, inline layman translations.
3. DO NOT rely solely on the synthetic `summary`; ensure the specific rationale comes from the `document`.

### Evaluation Rubric
* **Accessibility**: Can a reader with an 8th-grade reading level understand the exact constitutional issue?
* **Legal Precision**: Is the core holding of the court factually accurate to the raw document?
* **Scannability**: Is the formatting easily readable for an editor rushing to meet a news deadline?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Instantly translates 18,500-word, jargon-heavy Supreme Court verdicts into punchy, 8th-grade-level news briefs, perfectly suited for an editor on a tight deadline.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This task bypasses the persona's unfamiliarity with context limits and raw data parsing by acting as a highly efficient interpretive layer. By instructing the AI to use the synthetic 'summary' as a map but enforcing the raw 'document' as the ground truth, it mitigates inherited hallucinations. It applies journalistic constraints to force the extraction of a 'Bottom Line' and layman analogies, directly resolving the workflow friction of translating archaic text into accessible public communication.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your objective is to empower a non-technical, narrative-driven journalist to write Pulitzer-level editorial features on complex Supreme Court rulings. This task requires multi-dimensional synthesis and adversarial reasoning. You will audit an AI-generated summary against its massive ground-truth document, identify hidden legal frictions (such as dissenting or concurring opinions), and simulate the secondary societal effects of the ruling. You are delivering a complete, high-stakes editorial strategy pitch.

### Data Weighting
* **`document`**: GROUND TRUTH. You must actively look for nuances, dissenting views, and concurring limitations hidden deep within the text.
* **`summary`**: TREAT WITH SKEPTICISM. Audit this synthetic data for oversimplifications or omissions regarding the ruling's complexity.
* **`category`**: Use this as the definitive lens for projecting societal impact (e.g., 'Free Speech' implies projecting impacts on media, protests, or digital platforms).

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Adversarial Summary Audit**: Cross-reference the `summary` with the `document`. Identify at least one crucial nuance, concurring opinion, or dissent in the document that the summary completely missed or glossed over (e.g., Justice Harlan's differing rationale in Pointer v. Texas).
2. **Deconstruct the Friction**: Map the opposing legal philosophies present in the case. Why was this a difficult decision? What were the opposing arguments?
3. **Simulate the Ripple Effect**: Based on the `category` and the final ruling, project three distinct secondary effects this decision will have on society, industry, or future laws. 
4. **Formulate the Editorial Pitch**: Structure a comprehensive, narrative-driven pitch that the editor can immediately take to a publisher.

### Tone & Style
* **Voice**: Strategic, visionary, and deeply analytical.
* **Format**: Structured as a professional editorial pitch (Hook, Thesis, Narrative Arc).

### Content Requirements
* **The Blindspot**: A brief explanation of what the baseline summary missed.
* **The Friction**: A breakdown of the core ideological battle (Majority vs. Dissent/Concurrence).
* **The Ripple Effect**: 3 bulleted projections of how this case alters the legal/social landscape.
* **Editorial Narrative Arc**: A 3-act structure (The Origin, The Ruling, The Aftermath) for a feature-length article.

### Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
1. DO NOT assume unanimous agreement. Actively hunt for and highlight dissenting or concurring logic.
2. DO NOT output raw data or code snippets. The user has zero coding ability.
3. DO NOT use generic societal impacts; projections MUST be intrinsically tied to the specific `category` and ruling.

### Evaluation Rubric
* **Adversarial Depth**: Did the AI successfully identify a meaningful gap or oversimplification in the synthetic summary?
* **Strategic Value**: Are the 'Ripple Effect' projections plausible, insightful, and directly tied to the case's category?
* **Editorial Readiness**: Is the pitch structured in a way that an overwhelmed, non-technical editor can immediately utilize for an audience-facing narrative?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Cross-references full legal rulings with synthetic summaries to find hidden frictions, projecting societal ripple effects to generate a high-stakes, narrative-driven editorial pitch.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This high-complexity task leverages the AI to do the heavy lifting of adversarial reasoning and cross-referencing, shielding the non-technical persona from data processing tools. By explicitly forcing the LLM to audit the potentially flawed synthetic summary against the massive raw document, it actively mitigates AI bias and hallucination. Furthermore, it transforms dense legal friction into a 'Ripple Effect' simulation, handing the journalist a ready-to-publish narrative strategy that perfectly aligns with their business motivation for deep audience engagement.

task_1.judgement: Strong conceptual fit: the dataset’s full-text Supreme Court opinions (document) directly power a journalist-facing, de-jargonized news brief. The task smartly treats the synthetic summary as secondary and enforces ground-truth extraction, aligning with the schema’s structural logic. It addresses the persona’s no-code, speed-focused workflow and requires legally precise interpretation. Main feasibility risk is the extreme, variable document length and inconsistent section headers across cases, which may exceed context limits or hinder quick retrieval of the ‘Held’ and statutory anchors. The task would further benefit from a standardized output schema and explicit fallback heuristics when a Syllabus or ‘Held’ section is absent, plus a concrete confidence rubric tied to quoted evidence.
task_1.improvement_suggestion: Add retrieval heuristics and a structured output schema. Specifically: (1) Require locating sections by regex-style anchors: 'Syllabus', 'Held:', 'Opinion of the Court', 'It is so ordered', 'U.S.C.', 'Amendment'; if absent, fall back to first 1,500–3,000 words and any paragraph with 'Held' or statutory cites. (2) Mandate two short, verbatim quotes from the document: one naming the precise constitutional/statutory basis and one capturing the ruling rationale, with line/paragraph markers if available. (3) Output as strict JSON with keys: headline, conflict, ruling, bottom_line, analogy, anchors (constitutional_or_statutory), evidence_quotes, confidence. (4) Confidence rubric: High when the ruling and anchor are directly quoted from ‘Held’/majority; Medium when inferred from opinion text without a labeled ‘Held’; Low if only corroborated by the synthetic summary. This tightens grounding, improves scannability, and mitigates context-window variance.

task_2.judgement: Strong alignment overall. The dataset’s schema (document, summary, category, case/link) directly supports the task’s need to audit AI summaries against ground-truth opinions, surface doctrinal frictions (majority vs. concurrence/dissent), and translate outcomes into category-specific ripple effects. The task is editorially consequential and tailored to the journalist’s strengths (narrative, simplification) while shielding them from tooling and coding. It demands adversarial, multi-dimensional reasoning and explicitly centers the document as ground truth, which fits the schema’s structural logic. The only weakness is operational: documents can be extremely long, and the task does not specify a method for reliably locating dissents/concurrences and vote splits within such texts, which may strain context handling and risk partial coverage.
task_2.improvement_suggestion: Add a citation-first, length-aware audit protocol: require extraction of (a) vote split, (b) named author(s) of majority/concurrence/dissent, (c) holding and standard of review, and (d) 2–3 pinpoint citations to the opinion sections containing the key friction. Mandate a heading-based sweep (Syllabus → Majority → Concurrence(s) → Dissent(s)) to ensure coverage on very long documents. Constrain ripple effects to three category-tied projections each anchored to a specific legal change (rule announced or narrowed) in the holding. Conclude with an explicit Confidence & Coverage checklist confirming each required element is sourced from the document text.

tasks_info.task_name: Hierarchical Keyword Synthesis for CMS Ingestion
tasks_info.task_requirement:
## Strategic Intent
Your objective is to enhance Information Architecture (IA) accuracy and searchability for legal professionals. The current dataset relies on 27 overly broad categories (e.g., 'Search & Seizure') and synthetic summaries that often omit niche legal doctrines. As the backend intelligence for a graphical CMS, you must analyze the raw court documents to extract highly specific, granular metadata that bridges the gap between the broad category and the complex reality of the case.

## Data Weighting
* **`document` (Ground Truth):** Treat this as the definitive source. You must extract specific legal tests, exceptions, and doctrines directly from this text.
* **`summary` (Guide/Noise):** Use this for high-level context, but do not trust it to contain the specific niche keywords needed for sub-categorization.
* **`category` (Root Node):** Use this strictly as the top-level parent in your taxonomy tree.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Root Validation:** Identify the provided `category` and confirm its general applicability based on the `document`.
2. **Doctrine Extraction:** Scan the `document` for specific legal standards, tests, or exceptions (e.g., 'search incident to citation', 'in loco parentis', 'Mendenhall test').
3. **Contextual Tagging:** Identify the specific setting, actors, and physical objects involved (e.g., 'vehicle', 'high school', 'purse', 'fleeing suspect').
4. **Taxonomy Construction:** Map your findings into a strict hierarchical output designed for graphical UI ingestion: Root Category -> Sub-Category -> Niche Keywords.

## Tone & Style
Maintain the structured, methodical tone of an Information Architect and Metadata Strategist. Use precise legal terminology without resorting to data science or algorithmic jargon.

## Content Requirements
Your output must include:
* **Root Node:** The original category.
* **Proposed Sub-Categories:** 1 to 2 mid-level categories (e.g., 'Warrantless Vehicle Search').
* **Niche Tags:** 5 to 8 highly specific keywords/phrases extracted directly from the document.
* **UI Placement Recommendation:** A brief note on how these tags should be displayed in a graphical faceted search interface.

## Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
* [ ] DO NOT suggest algorithmic classification models or Python scripts.
* [ ] DO NOT rely solely on the `summary` for your keywords.
* [ ] DO NOT use generic tags (e.g., 'law', 'court', 'police').
* [ ] MUST include a Confidence Score (1-10) rating how explicitly the niche tags are defined in the raw document.

## Evaluation Rubric
1. **Precision:** Are the generated tags specific enough to distinguish between two cases in the same broad category?
2. **Fidelity:** Did the AI successfully bypass the summary's limitations by extracting exact doctrines from the raw document?
3. **CMS Readiness:** Is the hierarchical structure immediately usable by a non-technical metadata manager using a graphical UI?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Turn overly broad legal labels into highly specific, hierarchical metadata tags ready for graphical CMS ingestion, bypassing noisy AI summaries.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This task bridges the gap between a clunky, 27-label legacy taxonomy and the complex reality of Supreme Court cases. Knowing the persona cannot write classification algorithms, we use the LLM to act as the cognitive backend. The prompt forces the AI to ignore the potentially hallucinatory synthetic summary, dive into the massive raw document, and extract granular legal doctrines (like 'Mendenhall test'). This populates the user's graphical CMS with high-fidelity tags, instantly resolving workflow friction around searchability without requiring a single line of code.

tasks_info.task_name: Faceted Taxonomy Refactoring & Synthetic Noise Auditing
tasks_info.task_requirement:
## Strategic Intent
The current single-label classification system (e.g., assigning a case purely to 'Search & Seizure') creates severe bottlenecks for complex legal research. Furthermore, the synthetic `summary` data often homogenizes nuanced legal arguments, causing users to hit search dead-ends. Your mission is to audit the synthetic summary for critical omissions and architect a multi-dimensional, faceted taxonomy schema that captures the intersecting legal realities of the case.

## Data Weighting
* **`document` (Absolute Ground Truth):** The ultimate arbiter of fact and legal nuance.
* **`summary` (Adversarial Target):** Treat this as a potentially biased or incomplete transformation. Actively hunt for what it missed.
* **`category` (Legacy Constraint):** View this as a restrictive label that must be expanded into a multi-faceted profile.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Discrepancy Audit:** Cross-reference the `document` against the `summary`. Identify at least two critical legal nuances, dissenting arguments, or specific contextual factors present in the document but omitted or smoothed over in the summary.
2. **Faceted Architecture Design:** Break the case down into a 4-axis metadata schema suitable for a complex graphical CMS:
   - *Axis 1: Primary Legal Doctrine* (The core constitutional or statutory issue).
   - *Axis 2: Context/Setting* (Where it happened, who was involved).
   - *Axis 3: Evidentiary Focus* (What was seized or contested).
   - *Axis 4: Overlapping Domains* (Secondary legal categories the case touches, e.g., 'School/Education Law' overlapping with 'Search & Seizure').
3. **Search Simulation Scenario:** Write a brief use-case demonstrating how a legal researcher searching for a highly specific precedent would fail using the old `category` + `summary`, but succeed using your new Faceted Architecture.

## Tone & Style
Write as a Principal Information Architect conducting a critical system audit. Be analytical, uncompromising on data fidelity, and highly structured.

## Content Requirements
* **Audit Report:** Explicitly list the 'noise' or 'omissions' in the synthetic summary.
* **Faceted Schema Profile:** The 4-axis metadata breakdown with specific values for the case.
* **Search Simulation:** A paragraph contrasting the legacy search failure with the new schema's success.

## Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
* [ ] DO NOT accept the synthetic summary's narrative at face value; you must prove you read the raw document.
* [ ] DO NOT propose machine learning solutions; the output must be a data-modeling structure applicable to a graphical metadata management tool.
* [ ] DO NOT create overlapping or redundant tags across the 4 axes.

## Evaluation Rubric
1. **Adversarial Rigor:** Did the AI successfully identify meaningful gaps or noise in the synthetic summary compared to the raw document?
2. **Taxonomic Sophistication:** Are the 4 axes distinct, logically sound, and capable of resolving the single-label bottleneck?
3. **Practical Empathy:** Does the search simulation accurately reflect the workflow friction of a legal researcher, proving the value of the new architecture?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Audit synthetic summaries for critical omissions and redesign rigid single-category labels into a multi-dimensional, 4-axis faceted metadata schema.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This is a high-level architectural fix for systemic data modeling issues. The 27 legacy categories are too rigid for intersecting legal concepts (e.g., a case involving both schools and vehicle searches). This prompt forces the AI into an adversarial posture against the Cmd-R+ generated summaries to find lost nuances. It then refactors the data into a Faceted Taxonomy (Subject, Setting, Evidence, Overlap). Finally, it requires a 'Search Simulation' to validate that the new data structure actually solves the persona's business motivation: achieving flawless Information Architecture accuracy and searchability.

task_1.judgement: Strong alignment overall. The persona’s strengths in taxonomy design and metadata management directly leverage the dataset’s document and category fields. The task is pragmatic and high-value: replacing broad categories with doctrine-level facets improves search precision for legal professionals. The instructions correctly privilege the raw opinion text over the synthetic summary, acknowledging known noise. Minor feasibility risks arise from extreme document length and inconsistent opinion formatting, which are not fully mitigated in the task. Additionally, the prompt’s use of 'Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)' could be reframed to avoid demanding latent reasoning disclosure while still producing auditable outputs. With small additions—section anchoring, citation capture, and controlled vocabulary—the task would be immediately CMS-ready and highly reliable.
task_1.improvement_suggestion: Add enforceable evidence anchors and controlled facets. Require each niche tag to (a) cite the exact section header used (e.g., 'Syllabus', 'Held', 'Opinion of the Court', 'Dissent'), (b) include the first pinpoint citation or paragraph/character span from the document, and (c) map to a fixed mid-level facet set (Context, Actors, Legal Test/Standard, Procedural Posture, Authority Cited, Relief/Remedy). Also mandate Bluebook-style short cites for named tests/doctrines where available. This mitigates length variance, improves auditability, and yields immediately ingestible, de-duplicated CMS metadata without requiring code.

task_2.judgement: Strong alignment. The dataset’s columns (document as ground truth, summary as synthetic derivative, category as legacy label) map directly to the persona’s responsibilities in taxonomy design and metadata refinement via graphical tools. The task is feasible using only the provided schema and explicitly avoids ML or coding, focusing instead on faceted modeling and adversarial review of summaries. It addresses a substantive business pain point—single-label bottlenecks and homogenized summaries undermining search—and requires high-level interpretive rigor. The only caveat is operational feasibility at scale given extreme document length variance, which necessitates a triage and citation-anchoring protocol to ensure reliable discrepancy audits.
task_2.improvement_suggestion: Add a citation-anchored audit workflow to manage long opinions: for each identified omission and every selected facet value, require (a) a pinpoint citation or paragraph range from 'document' and (b) a short supporting quote (≤300 chars). Pair this with controlled vocabularies for each of the 4 axes (mutually exclusive within-axis terms), an omission severity scale (minor/contextual/critical), and a triage rule (sample syllabus + majority + concurrences/dissents first for >50k chars). This keeps the task fully GUI-executable, enhances data fidelity, and ensures non-overlapping, defensible facet assignments at scale.
